## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Mahākhandhaka* ("The Great Chapter") is the first chapter of the *Mahāvagga* in the Khandhaka section of the Vinaya Piṭaka [SuttaCentral; Norman 1983]. It is framed around the biographical narrative of Gautama Buddha immediately following his awakening at the Bodhi tree, extending up to the conversion of the jaṭilas and the formal admission of Sāriputta and Moggallāna into the monastic community [Norman 1983; Freedman 1977]. Within this narrative setting, three major early discourses are recorded in full: the *Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta* (Setting in Motion the Wheel of the Teaching), the *Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta* (Characteristics of Non-Self), and the *Ādittapariyāya Sutta* (The Fire Sermon) [SuttaCentral; Norman 1983]. The text applies the designation *arahant* to the Buddha's first seven liberated disciples [Freedman 1977]. As followers multiply, the chapter details the phased institutional establishment of the Buddhist monastic order, introducing the rules and procedures for formal ordination (*pabbajjā* and *upasampadā*), candidate qualifications and exclusions, novice training, and the structured reciprocal duties between preceptors (*upajjhāya* and *ācariya*) and their pupils [SuttaCentral; Freedman 1977; Rhys Davids & Oldenberg 1881; Ānandajoti 2010].

Scholars consider this text central to the development of canonical Buddha biographies, which originated within Vinaya literature [Hirakawa 1990]. The *Mahākhandhaka* corresponds to the *Pravrajyāvastu* ("Chapter on Going Forth") preserved in Northern Vinaya traditions, such as the Dharmaguptaka and Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinayas, while parallel narrative accounts appear in the Sanskrit *Mahāvastu* of the Lokottaravādins, the Mūlasarvāstivādin *Saṅghabhedavastu*, and the *Catuṣpariṣatsūtra* (preserved in the Sarvāstivādin Dīrghāgama) [Hirakawa 1990; Norman 1983; Dutt 1925; Bapat & Hirakawa 1970]. Sanskrit manuscript fragments matching the Pali *Mahākhandhaka* were identified by Louis Finot in the Pelliot collection and among Turfan finds [Andrews et al. 2015; Norman 1983]. Its opening narrative also parallels the introductory discourses of the *Udāna* (Ud 1.1–1.3) and episodes in the *Lalitavistara* [Norman 1983; Ānandajoti 2010; SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus corroborates extensive text reuse within the Pali canon across other Khandhakas (notably Kd 18, Kd 20, Kd 6, Kd 8, and Kd 2), the *Vinayasaṅgaha-aṭṭhakathā*, and Nikāya discourses (such as DN 14, SN 22, SN 35, and AN 5), while automatically aligning passages with the Sanskrit *Saṅghabhedavastu*, *Mahāvastu*, *Catuṣpariṣatsūtra*, and the Tibetan *Vinayavastu* [DharmaNexus]. Complete English translations include those by I. B. Horner and Bhikkhu Brahmali, with sections 1–4 translated separately by Bhikkhu Ānandajoti [SuttaCentral; Ānandajoti 2010].
